front: The crude birth rate: births per 1,000 people a year.
cue: Comparing how fast places add people by birth.
formula: <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>CBR</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{CBR}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>births in a year</mtext><mtext>population</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{births in a year}}{\text{population}} \times 1{,}000</annotation></semantics></math>
worked: <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{30{,}000}{1{,}000{,}000} \times 1{,}000</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>30</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext> per </mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 30\,\text{ per }1{,}000</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: It is per 1,000 people, not a percent, and not per woman (that is the total fertility rate).

front: The rate of natural increase: the percent a population grows each year from births minus deaths.
cue: Reading growth from the two crude rates.
trap: Migration is not in it, and the order is births minus deaths. Divide by 10 to turn "per 1,000" into a percent.

front: Doubling time by the rule of 70: about how many years a population takes to double at its current rate of natural increase.
cue: Turning a growth rate into a time.
trap: Use the RNI as a percent (2, not 0.02). A population that is not growing has no doubling time.

front: The net migration rate: people gained or lost by migration, per 1,000 people a year.
cue: Adding migration to natural increase to see total growth.
worked: <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{6{,}000 - 2{,}000}{1{,}000{,}000} \times 1{,}000</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>4</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext> per </mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 4\,\text{ per }1{,}000</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: More people leaving than arriving gives a negative rate.

front: The dependency ratio: people of the ages that usually depend on others, per 100 people of working age.
cue: Reading the strain a population pyramid shows: many children, many older people, or both.
formula: <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>dependency ratio</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{dependency ratio}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext>under </mtext><mn>15</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>65</mn><mtext> and over</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn><mtext> to </mtext><mn>64</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{under }15 + 65\text{ and over}}{15\text{ to }64} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: The working-age group (15 to 64) goes on the bottom. Youth and elderly ratios use one group each.

front: The sex ratio: males per 100 females.
cue: Reading the two sides of a population pyramid.
trap: Above 100 means more males. It changes with age: women live longer on average.

front: Arithmetic density: people per unit of all the land.
cue: A first comparison of crowding between places.
formula: <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>arithmetic density</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{arithmetic density}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>population</mtext><mtext>total land area</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{population}}{\text{total land area}}</annotation></semantics></math>
worked: <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.25em"></mspace><msup><mtext>km</mtext><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1{,}000{,}000}{50{,}000\ \text{km}^2}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>20</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext> per km</mtext><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 20\,\text{ per km}^2</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: It hides where people live: deserts and mountains count as land.

front: Physiological density: people per unit of farmland, the pressure on the land that grows food.
cue: Judging how hard a country's farmland must work.
worked: <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.25em"></mspace><msup><mtext>km</mtext><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1{,}000{,}000}{5{,}000\ \text{km}^2}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>200</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext> per km</mtext><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 200\,\text{ per km}^2</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: The bottom is arable land only. Do not confuse it with carrying capacity, which is how many people land can support.

front: Agricultural density: farmers per unit of farmland.
cue: A clue to how mechanized farming is: fewer farmers per unit usually means more machines.
worked: <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.25em"></mspace><msup><mtext>km</mtext><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{100{,}000}{5{,}000\ \text{km}^2}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>20</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext> per km</mtext><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 20\,\text{ per km}^2</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: The top is farmers, not everyone.

front: The rank-size rule: the city of rank n has about 1/n the population of the largest city.
cue: Checking whether a country's cities follow the rule or have a primate city.
trap: A primate city is far larger than the rule predicts for rank 1 against rank 2.

front: The gravity model: interaction between two places rises with their populations and falls with the square of the distance between them.
cue: Comparing which pair of cities will have more trips, calls or trade.
trap: Square the distance. Twice as far means a quarter of the interaction, not half.

front: Percent change: how much a value grew or shrank, as a share of where it started.
cue: Reading a table of populations or outputs over time.
trap: Divide by the old value, not the new one.

front: A ratio scale (1:50,000) turns a map length into a ground distance: 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm on the ground.
formula: <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>ground distance</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{ground distance}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>map distance</mtext><mo>×</mo><mtext>scale denominator</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{map distance} \times \text{scale denominator}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: A large-scale map (1:10,000) shows a small area in detail; a small-scale map (1:10,000,000) shows a large area. Map scale is not the scale of analysis.
